observations.mechanism: Both the oversized DB connection pool (finding 1) and the per‑request creation of an httpx.AsyncClient (finding 5) consume the same worker process pool; when DB connections are exhausted and HTTP clients cannot be reused, workers remain blocked.
observations.consequence: The service can run out of available workers, causing request time‑outs and a noticeable drop in throughput.

observations.mechanism: The missing propagation of the request correlation ID (finding 4) combined with the swallowed exception that returns an empty list (finding 2) means the silent failure cannot be linked to its request in the logs.
observations.consequence: Silent errors become invisible to operators, making root‑cause analysis harder and increasing mean time to repair.

observations.mechanism: Creating a new AsyncClient per request without a timeout (finding 5) and configuring the AsyncClient with timeout=None (finding 10) both allow a slow upstream to hold a worker indefinitely.
observations.consequence: Workers can be tied up for unbounded periods, leading to worker‑pool exhaustion and sporadic latency spikes.

observations.mechanism: Instantiating a fresh httpx.AsyncClient for each call (findings 5 and 6) forces a cold TLS handshake on every external request, incurring DNS, TCP and TLS round‑trips each time.
observations.consequence: The cumulative latency added by these handshakes degrades overall request latency, especially under load.

observations.mechanism: The hard‑coded DATABASE_URL credentials (finding 3) are the same variable used by the DB engine whose pool size is mis‑configured (finding 1), linking a secret‑management flaw with a connection‑pool capacity issue.
observations.consequence: The service simultaneously risks credential leakage and DB‑connection saturation, threatening both security and availability.
